DELIVERABLE: Give an agent the create_calendar_event spec plus the failed-call transcripts, ask why those calls went wrong and what the description leaves ambiguous, then rewrite the description so start must be an RFC 3339 timestamp with UTC offset and attendees must be email addresses, and rerun the same tasks against the revised description.
BOUNDARY: Do not ship the proxy that quietly guesses timezones and resolves names (it hides the errors and can book the wrong hour), and do not rely on prompt reminders.
EVIDENCE: Compare the bad-start and bad-attendee call rate on the same task set before and after the description change; the 30% should drop.

DELIVERABLE: Hand an agent the tool spec and the transcripts of the failed calls, have it explain why they failed and what is missing, update the tool description to demand an ISO 8601 start with offset and attendee emails, then rerun the identical failing tasks.
BOUNDARY: No silent proxy and no extra system-prompt warnings; errors should stay visible and fixes belong in the description.
EVIDENCE: Same tasks, before versus after: fraction of calls with a valid offset and valid emails.

DELIVERABLE: Add a short rule to the system prompt reminding agents to include a UTC offset and use email addresses, put the proxy in front of the tool to normalize times and resolve names, and make the tool return clearer validation errors.
BOUNDARY: Keep the tool description short; the agent should not see timezone handling at all.
EVIDENCE: Watch the weekly error rate after the proxy ships.

DELIVERABLE: Take the tool spec and the 40 failed-call transcripts, ask an agent why each run_sql call failed and what the description is missing or ambiguous, rewrite the description to say it is PostgreSQL (double-quoted identifiers, no backticks) and that queries on the 90M-row table must be bounded with LIMIT or a filter, then rerun the same tasks.
BOUNDARY: A 'SQL rules' block in every system prompt is not the fix; the tool contract itself has to carry the guidance.
EVIDENCE: Same tasks before versus after: statement-timeout rate and dialect-error rate.

DELIVERABLE: Feed the spec and the failure transcripts to an agent, ask what in the description invites backticks and unbounded SELECT *, update it to state Postgres syntax and require a LIMIT or WHERE clause, and replay the same failing tasks.
BOUNDARY: Prompt-level reminders are not a substitute for fixing the description.
EVIDENCE: Count timeouts and syntax errors on the replayed tasks against the 40 logged failures.

DELIVERABLE: Add a SQL rules reminder to the system prompt: use Postgres syntax, no backticks, always add LIMIT; also have a wrapper append a default LIMIT 1000 to every query.
BOUNDARY: Keep the tool description unchanged to avoid churn.
EVIDENCE: Check the timeout count next week.

DELIVERABLE: Give an agent the search_logs spec plus the 55 failure transcripts, ask why the calls failed and what is ambiguous, revise the description to say pattern is a glob not a regex and that since is required to bound the time window, then rerun the same tasks against it.
BOUNDARY: Do not wait for a model upgrade or ship renamed parameters without diagnosing why agents misread the current ones.
EVIDENCE: Same tasks, before and after: share of calls that use a glob and a bounded since window.

DELIVERABLE: Hand an agent the spec and the failed transcripts and ask what in the description misleads it about regex versus glob and about the time range; update the description accordingly and re-run those same failing tasks.
BOUNDARY: Renaming parameters alone could repeat the confusion; the description must be fixed first.
EVIDENCE: Replay the same tasks and compare the too-many-results error rate.

DELIVERABLE: Ship v2 with parameters renamed to glob and window, set a default window of 24h, and revisit if the next model upgrade does not fix the remaining mistakes.
BOUNDARY: Skip reading the old failures since v2 changes the interface anyway.
EVIDENCE: Track the too-many-results error count after launch.

DELIVERABLE: No. Characters per token depends on the tokenizer and the content (English prose, code, JSON and non-Latin scripts differ), so divide-by-four drifts and can undercount by a wide margin; for any budget that matters, count with the provider's tokenizer or token-counting API instead.
BOUNDARY: Fine as a rough order-of-magnitude sketch, never as a limit check.
EVIDENCE: Compare the estimate with the API's token count on a sample of your real content.

DELIVERABLE: The ratio varies by language and content type and by tokenizer, so it is only a ballpark and can badly undercount code or Korean. Run text through the vendor's tokenizer to get the real number.
BOUNDARY: Not safe for budget-critical decisions.
EVIDENCE: Sample a few real documents and check the estimate against the counted tokens.

DELIVERABLE: Roughly yes for English prose: about four characters per token, so divide by four and keep a 20% safety margin. Code and non-English text usually take more tokens, so widen the margin for those.
BOUNDARY: Do not expect exact numbers.
EVIDENCE: Spot-check with a few documents.

DELIVERABLE: The 3.5 ratio is an English figure; Korean and source code tokenize very differently, so the cap will drift and likely undercount tokens, letting prompts overflow; replace it by counting with the provider's tokenizer or token-counting API.
BOUNDARY: A sizing helper still gates real requests, so 'conceptual' does not excuse an unmeasured ratio.
EVIDENCE: Run a sample of the Korean and Python inputs through the token-counting API and compare with window_tokens * 3.5.

DELIVERABLE: Flag it: chars per token differs by language and content, so 3.5 is wrong for Korean and code. Use the vendor's tokenizer to count tokens before truncating.
BOUNDARY: Even a rough helper needs the real tokenizer once it decides what gets truncated.
EVIDENCE: Measured token counts on a few real files versus the estimate.

DELIVERABLE: Make the ratio language-aware: roughly 1.5 characters per token for Korean and 3 for code, and leave 15% headroom under the window.
BOUNDARY: Fine as a helper, not a billing calculation.
EVIDENCE: Check a couple of inputs by hand.

DELIVERABLE: Not far: 1.33 tokens per word is an English-prose rule of thumb, and Spanish and JSON tool traces tokenize differently, so the forecast can be materially off; count a representative sample with the provider's token-counting API and scale from that.
BOUNDARY: Treat the sheet as an order-of-magnitude figure until it is calibrated.
EVIDENCE: Run a week of real chats through the token-counting API and compare tokens per word with 1.33.

DELIVERABLE: It varies with language and content, so JSON and Spanish usually produce more tokens per word than 1.33 and the sheet will drift. Calibrate it with the provider's tokenizer on real samples.
BOUNDARY: Okay for a sanity check, not for budget lines.
EVIDENCE: Counted tokens on real chats versus the sheet's estimate.

DELIVERABLE: It is a reasonable ballpark for English, but Spanish and JSON likely take more tokens per word, so bump the multiplier to about 1.6 and add a 15% buffer to the forecast.
BOUNDARY: Revisit the multiplier quarterly.
EVIDENCE: Compare against last month's invoice.

DELIVERABLE: Measure the static-vs-dynamic token split (always-loaded prompt and index tokens versus tokens pulled in from runbook files per incident) and, from per-run read logs, how often each dynamically loaded runbook is actually used (read rate per file and share of loaded tokens that were referenced).
BOUNDARY: Do not judge it by prompt-size reduction alone; a smaller prompt proves nothing if files are loaded but never used or the index fails to route.
EVIDENCE: Log every runbook read with its incident ID, aggregate per-file usage over a few weeks, and compare static and dynamic token totals.

DELIVERABLE: Track two numbers: the split between static tokens (system prompt plus index) and dynamic tokens loaded from files, and the usage rate, meaning how often loaded runbooks are really used in the answer. Instrument file reads per run to get both.
BOUNDARY: Prompt size going from 18K to a few K is not evidence on its own.
EVIDENCE: A per-run log of runbook reads joined with token counts.

DELIVERABLE: Evaluate on task success and latency: run the same incidents with eager and on-demand loading and compare resolution rate, time to resolve, and total tokens per incident.
BOUNDARY: Avoid judging on prompt size only.
EVIDENCE: Two weeks of incidents for each arm.

DELIVERABLE: A 30% drop in total tokens does not settle it: break tokens into the static share (prompt plus file index) and the dynamic share (policy files loaded per conversation), measure how often each loaded policy file is actually used in the answer, and confirm resolution rate and answer quality did not fall.
BOUNDARY: Total tokens per conversation can fall because the agent skips the files it needs; that would be a regression, not a win.
EVIDENCE: Per-conversation file-read logs, a usage count for each of the 60 files, and resolution rate before and after.

DELIVERABLE: Check three things: static versus dynamic token split, the usage rate of the files the bot loads (how often a loaded file is really used), and whether task success held. Without those the 30% only shows the prompt shrank.
BOUNDARY: Fewer tokens may mean fewer files read, not better routing.
EVIDENCE: File-access logs per conversation and CSAT before versus after.

DELIVERABLE: Check that the 30% is significant across conversation types, that latency did not rise, and that resolution rate and CSAT held steady after the switch.
BOUNDARY: Do not credit the change if escalations went up.
EVIDENCE: Dashboard cohorts split by topic.

DELIVERABLE: First add logging so you can decide on data: record the static-vs-dynamic token split and how often each of the 35 playbooks is actually opened and used per task over a few weeks; then prune or merge playbooks that are never opened and promote the heavily used ones into the static prompt instead of reverting wholesale.
BOUNDARY: 'The agent never seems to open them' is an anecdote; with no logging nobody knows the usage rate, and loading all 35 would add their full token cost to every request.
EVIDENCE: Per-file open counts and token totals split static versus dynamic, collected before any revert.

DELIVERABLE: Instrument playbook reads, then compare the static share of tokens with the dynamic share and the usage rate per file. Playbooks used often should move into the always-loaded prompt; ones never read should be removed or merged.
BOUNDARY: Reverting without usage data trades a guess for a certain token cost.
EVIDENCE: A few weeks of read logs with per-file frequency.

DELIVERABLE: Revert only if task accuracy drops: run an A/B with all 35 playbooks in the prompt versus on demand for two weeks and compare accuracy and cost.
BOUNDARY: Keep the playbook text unchanged during the test.
EVIDENCE: Accuracy and cost per arm.
